Issued at 419 PM CDT Fri Jul 24 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/UNCERTAINTIES/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS:
Honestly, it was this forecaster's first true 7-day forecast
shift in a while, so am admittedly lacking much "personal
history" with recent trends. Overall though, a quick comparison
of our previous (overnight shift) forecast to this latest one
reveals primarily minor/limited changes. 

Temperature and heat index wise: 
If anything, expected peak heat index values have crept a touch
higher for Saturday (remaining similar for Sunday-Monday).
Barring any unforeseen cloud issues and/or outflow boundaries
getting in the mix, all three afternoons/early evenings should
feature widespread peak heat index 100-110, with at least
localized spots mainly within Nebraska counties east of Hwy 281
(where dewpoints/humidity will be highest) at least briefly 
creeping above 110 heat index. Although 110+ is technically our 
Extreme Heat Warning criteria, at least for now we are calling 
for small enough of an area to breach 110+ for only a limited 
amount of time...that was comfortable just keeping a Heat 
Advisory in place through all three days at this time. 

Rain/thunderstorm potential:
As touched on in Key Messages above, parts of the Saturday
night-Sunday night time frame might not be truly "guaranteed"
dry...despite our lack of official mentionable rain chances in
our official forecast (which need to be 15+% to be included).
Although still over 48 hours away and carrying a high degree of
uncertainty, what likely bears most watching is Sunday evening-
overnight, during which time there is limited model support
(albeit including the often-reliable ECMWF) for thunderstorm to
TRY slipping into our mainly our far northern/northeast
counties. IF this occurs, probably cannot rule out the potential
for a strong to marginally-severe storm, and we'll acknowledge
here that SPC has introduced a Marginal Risk of severe (level 1
of 5) to some of our northern/northeast counties on their latest
Day 3 Outlook. 


- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL RUNDOWN (through Fri. July 31):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SITUATION AS OF 330 PM:
Once the last of any spotty measurable showers moved out by
around sunrise this morning, the main question today was how
efficiently an expansive lower stratus cloud deck would clear,
and the resultant impact on temps. In short, the low stratus has
proven slower/more stubborn to clear across especially the
majority of our Nebraska CWA, with cloudy/mostly cloudy
conditions still hanging tough at this time in most places, in
turn keeping current temps in the 70s. In fairly sharp contrast,
no worse than partly cloudy (if not mostly sunny) skies have
prevailed this afternoon within our KS zones along with some of
our western-most Nebraska counties (such as Dawson/Furnas),
allowing temps to quickly rise into the 80s and even low 90s.

As we get into late afternoon/evening, clouds should continue to
SLOWLY scatter out/break up from west-to-east and south-to-
north, but probably not in time to get our entire 
central/eastern CWA into the 80s as earlier expected (if nothing
else, official daytime highs will likely be later-than-usual). 

In the big picture of the mid-upper levels, water vapor
satellite and short term model data confirm that we remain under
northwesterly flow aloft, directed between a prominent upper
ridge/high centered over the Four Corners region, and a broad
trough positioned from the Great Lakes region into the 
northeast states. At the surface, the pressure gradient is 
weak...keeping wind speeds mainly well under 10 MPH across the 
majority of our CWA..with direction mainly from the south-
southeast. 


- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
Although a few showers could try developing slightly east of our
CWA generally along eastern parts of the NE/KS border area,
confidence is fairly high in our going dry forecast. That leaves
the evolution of low clouds and/or fog as the "million dollar
question" for tonight. As already mentioned, low clouds have
been slower to clear today in many central/eastern counties, and
latest RAP low-level RH fields suggest some of our eastern-most
Nebraska counties might struggle to clear until closer to 10-11
PM. This raises some concern that fog could develop earlier than
currently expected tonight...possibly favoring the western edge
of the "clearing line". However, our official forecast is geared
more toward the latest HRRR solutions, which keeps us largely
fog-free until post-midnight...after which time at least a
50-mile wide corridor of fog (perhaps dense?) could materialize
in generally west-southwest to east-northeast fashion across
parts of our CWA (currently most favoring central areas). That
